An Overview of Go's Tooling: Version 2

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 40 min read (8087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alexedwards

⏱️ ~40 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My newly introduced book guides you through the start-to-finish build of a real world web application in Go — covering topics like how to structure your code, manage dependencies, create dynamic database-driven pages, and how to authenticate and authorize users securely.
  • Industry observers note that way back in 2019, I wrote the blog post An Overview of Go's Tooling.
  • But a lot has changed in the past 7 years, and some of the information in that original post is now painfully out-of-date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My newly introduced book guides you through the start-to-finish build of a real world web application in Go — covering topics like how to structure your code, manage dependencies, create dynamic database-driven pages, and how to authenticate and authorize users securely.

Black Friday sale: 30% off until the 1st December!

Industry observers note that way back in 2019, I wrote the blog post An Overview of Go's Tooling. It was a popular article and IIRC, ended up being one of the most-read items in the Go Weekly newsletter that year. It's also one that I personally still come back to fairly often, when I want to remind myself of a specific command that I can't remember.

But a lot has changed in the past 7 years, and some of the information in that original post is now painfully out-of-date. So this is a version 2 of that post... fully updated for the module-enabled, gopls-integrated, token-fuelled world that we now live in 😊.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest improvements to Go's tooling has been the introduction of fresh ways to run third-party tools. We now have three options — go install, go run, and go tool — each suited to slightly different use cases.

Recent findings suggest that the first option is to install the tool on your local machine using the go install command. You can run this command from anywhere on your machine, and it will download the necessary source code for the tool and create an executable binary in your GOBIN directory. So long as your GOBIN directory is on your system path, you can then run the tool whenever you need it.

For example, to install the latest version of govulncheck, check its install location, and run it, you can do this:.

It has been revealed that using go install tends to be a good option for general-purpose tools that happen to be written in Go, where you don't need to pin a specific version for use within a project or necessarily keep up with the latest release. Personally, I tend to use it for installing tools like hey, which I often use for things outside of Go development.

Sources indicate that the second option is to use go run to execute a specific version of a tool without installing it. For example, to run the latest version of govulncheck you can use the following command:.

I've written in detail about using go run to execute tools previously in this post, but this option is really useful when there is a tool you want to promptly run on an ad hoc basis.

Personally, I often use go run in this way during code reviews, when I want to do a one-time run of a specific static analysis tool using the latest version.

According to recent reports, I also find this approach useful in small solo projects where I don't have to worry about tool version differences with other developers. I'll often create a Makefile which uses go run to execute the latest version of code-quality tools — similar to this.

Lastly, there is now the option to add a tool as a module tool dependency to your go.mod file. At a very high level, you can use the go get -tool command to add the tool as a module dependency, and the necessary version information and checksums will be added to the go.mod and go.sum files. For example:.

And then you can run the specific version of the tool listed in the go.mod file with the go tool command, like so:.

This is a great option when you are working with a team of people, where for consistency and reproducibility you want to make sure that everyone is using exactly the same version of a tool.

I've previously written a much more detailed tutorial about how to use the go tool functionality, and I recommend checking that out for more information.

It has been revealed that another major development in recent years has been gopls. This is the official language server for Go, which you can use with any text editor or IDE that supports the Language Server Protocol (LSP).

If you're not already familiar with LSP, it's essentially a protocol that allows text editors to communicate with external programs called language servers, which act as the "brain" behind smart editor features.

The Go language server supports a wide range of smart editor features, including:.

To use gopls, the first thing you need to do is install it on your computer using the go install command, like so:.

Once gopls is installed, you then need to configure your editor to use it.

If you're using Zed or Helix, they should automatically detect gopls on your machine and start using it without any additional setup.

Sources indicate that if you're using VS Code, you'll need to install the official Go extension. To do this, open the Extensions Panel, search for golang.go, and install this extension. After you restart and open a .go file, you should see a lightning bolt next to the Go version in the status bar at the bottom of your editor. This indicates that the language server is running.

Sources indicate that for other editors, the steps are a little more complicated. Please see the official setup steps for Vim and Neovim, Emacs and Sublime Text.

Once your editor is configured, you should see smart editor features become available. For example, here's a screenshot of documentation when hovering over the http.Error() function in VS Code.

It has been revealed that the go doc tool remains the de facto way to view the documentation for standard library packages in your terminal. You can use it to view the documentation for an entire package, or for a specific type, function or method. For example:.

You can also use the -src flag to view the relevant source code:.

Since Go 1.25, you can also use the -http flag to start a documentation server and browse the documentation locally in your web browser. For example, to view documentation for the bytes package in your browser you can run the following command:.

To display information about your current Go operating environment, you can use the go env command. This can be particularly useful if you're working on an unfamiliar machine.

Recent findings suggest that if there are specific values that you're interested in, you can pass them as arguments to go env. For example:.

To show documentation for all go env variables and values you can run:.

If you have your text editor setup to use gopls, there is a good chance that your .go files will automatically be formatted according to the Go conventions each time they are saved, as well as having their import lines automatically added, removed and sorted as necessary.

Recent findings suggest that if you're not using gopls, or you want to format files outside of your text editor (for example, as part of a pre-commit hook or CI pipeline), you can use the gofmt tool to format them. For example:.

Industry observers note that in these commands, the -w flag instructs the tool to rewrite files in place, the -s instructs the tool to apply certain simplifications to the code, and the -d flag instructs the tool to output diffs of the changes. If you want to only display the names of changed files, instead of diffs, you can swap this for the -l flag instead. Note that gofmt works recursively, so if you pass it a directory like . or ./cmd/foo it'll format all .go files within that directory tree.

Alternatively, you can run the go fmt command — which is essentially a wrapper around gofmt -l -w — like so:.

It has been revealed that often, as part of a quality audit check in a CI pipeline, I want to check that .go files are formatted correctly, without actually changing anything. To do this, I usually run gofmt -l . and check that the output from this command is empty. There's an example of this in the audit check in this Makefile.

It's also worth mentioning the goimports tool, which formats your .go files in the same way as gofmt, but also updates your import lines — adding, removing and sorting the lines as necessary. You can run it like so:.

You can use the go mod tidy command to automatically add missing dependencies to, and prune unused dependencies from, your go.mod and go.sum modfiles based on the imports in your .go files.

Sources indicate that it's a good idea to run this periodically to keep your modfiles synchronized with your code. Personally, I try to run this before each commit to make it easier to see exactly which code changes were responsible for adding or removing a dependency when looking through the version control history.

If you want to check if the modfiles are synchronized without actually changing them, you can use the -diff flag like so:.

This is a really useful command to use in audit checks and CI pipelines, because when you run it with -diff it will print out any changes and then exit with a non-zero code. If no changes are needed, it will exit with code 0.

Recent findings suggest that it's also worth mentioning that running go mod tidy ensures your modfiles include the dependencies needed across all possible build tag, OS and architecture combinations. Commands like go run, go test and go build are more selective, and only require dependencies for the current build configuration. This is why you might sometimes see additional lines appear in your modfiles unexpectedly when running go mod tidy.

For debugging Go applications, the standard tool to use is Delve. It allows you to set breakpoints, step through your code line by line, and do things like inspecting the values of variables and viewing the current call stack.

You can install Delve by running:.

According to recent reports, nowadays, the easiest way to use Delve is generally via the debugger integration in your text editor. For example, in VS Code you set breakpoints by clicking in the gutter next to a line of code, start a debugging session by opening the 'Run and Debug' panel, and use the debugging toolbar to step through your application and inspect what's happening as it runs.

According to recent reports, it's also possible to use Delve outside of a text editor and start an interactive debugging session in your terminal. For example, assuming you installed Delve using the go install command above, you could start debugging an application in the ./cmd/web directory by running:.

You can then use Delve's commands to set breakpoints, continue execution, step through your code, and inspect variables, in much the same way as in a text editor.

There is a nice introduction on how to use the terminal-based debugger in this post, and more information about debugging with Delve can be found in the official Delve documentation.

According to recent reports, go 1.26 made major changes to the go fix command, updating it so that it now automatically 'modernizes' your code to use the latest Go idioms and standard library APIs. When you run it, it will do things like replacing interface{} with any, and rewrite code to use functions like slices.Contains() rather than manual loops.

You can see a complete list of the analyzers that go fix supports, and what they do, by running go tool fix help:.

At its most basic, you can use go fix like this:.

In a recent development, however, it's vital to be aware that go fix will silently rewrite your .go files in place. If you want to know in advance what changes it will make without actually applying them you can use the -diff flag like so:.

Sometimes, when looking at the diff, you might decide that you want to make some, but not all, of the changes. For example, there have been times when I've decided that my original code was clearer without the modernizations applied by the embedlit and mapsloop analyzers. You can disable specific analyzers individually like so:.

In a recent development, since the release of gopls, the simplest, safest and most flexible way to refactor your code is by using its code transformation features in your text editor. For example, you can inline function calls, extract code into a function, rename identifiers, and move or remove parameters across your codebase, all in a few clicks.

For example, in VS Code you can use the 'Rename' and 'Refactor' options in the right-click menu to refactor code like so:.

More information, including a description of all supported refactoring features, can be found in the official gopls documentation.

However, if you don't want to use gopls, or are using a text editor that doesn't support it, you can still use gofmt with the -r flag to implement a rewrite rule that can assist with certain refactoring tasks. I've written more about this in my 2019 blog post on Go tooling here.

There are a few live reloading tools available for Go, which you can use to automatically rebuild and restart an application whenever certain files change. These are especially useful when developing web services, because they let you make changes to your code or template markup and then check the results in a browser without having to manually restart the application each time.

Sources indicate that the most mature and popular live reloading tool for Go is air-verse/air. You can run it using settings in a TOML configuration file , like so:.

Or you can configure it using command-line flags. For example, to watch all directories and rebuild the ./cmd/web application whenever a file with an extension in the set .go, .tmpl, .css, .js or .sql changes, you could use the following command:.

Here's a video illustrating the air live reloading functionality when developing a web application:.

It has been revealed that go's language server, gopls, includes an experimental MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes some of its functionality to AI coding assistants (such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex). This effectively allows the assistants to leverage the same "smart features" that your text editor has access to, rather than just relying on reading your files.

Assuming that you have gopls installed, you can configure your AI coding assistant to use the gopls MCP server by following the instructions in the official Go MCP documentation.

You can also run the gopls mcp -instructions command to get guidance for using the MCP server, which you can then provide to your coding assistant. For example:.

Sources indicate that another MCP server worth mentioning is mrjoshuak/godoc-mcp. This allows AI coding assistants to look up Go package documentation directly, which can be more token-efficient than reading through source files. You may wish to try this if you're using AI assistants heavily and want to reduce token usage.

In late 2022 the Go team released govulncheck, which checks your codebase against the Go vulnerability database to find known vulnerabilities in any standard library packages or third-party dependencies that you're using.

Unlike many other vulnerability scanners, it only flags vulnerabilities that actually affect you... meaning that a vulnerability in a part of a package that your code doesn't use won't be flagged.

It's an excellent tool, and I recommend running it routinely before you deploy a newly introduced version of your application to production.

Long term, the strategy is for govulncheck to become part of the main go command, but for now you can run it like so:.

Sources indicate that another really helpful tool is gosec, a static analyzer that looks for potential security problems in your code. You can run it like so:.

Industry observers note that in my experience it's not uncommon for gosec to flag challenges which on further inspection are false positives in the context of your specific codebase, or where you are deliberately using something insecure. When this happens, you can annotate the specific code with a #nosec comment to instruct gosec to omit it from future reports. For example:.

The venerable go vet command should still be your first port of call when it comes to static code analysis. It runs a relatively small set of checks, but the checks have a high signal-to-noise ratio and if go vet reports an issue, then it's very likely to be a problem you should address.

It's normally best to run go vet with its default settings, like so:.

You can see a complete list of the checks that go vet runs in the 'Registered analyzers' section of the help documentation:.

And you can also disable specific analyzers if you don't want their checks to run. For example, to disable the composites analyzer, which checks for unkeyed composite literals, you can run go vet like so:.

The staticcheck tool is kind of like go vet on steroids. It carries out around 160 different checks on your code — the vast majority of which are related to code correctness and performance, although it also includes a handful of checks for for 'stylistic' concerns like comment formatting too.

The complete list of checks, along with their respective ID codes and descriptions, can be found here.

It's crucial to note that staticcheck does not run all checks by default — only a subset of them. But you can configure exactly which checks are run using either the -checks command-line flag or a config file. For example:.

The nilaway tool is really useful for finding potential nil-pointer panics in your code. It's similar to the older nilness tool in what it aims to do, but is more comprehensive in its checks.

If you're not worried about nil-pointer panics in your test code, and only want to check your production code, you can also run it with the -exclude-test-files flag enabled. Like so:.

The errcheck tool has been around for a long time (14 years!), and it remains a great way to check for unhandled errors in your code.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

It has been revealed that it's worth mentioning that, by default, errcheck only reports errors which are completely unhandled. It doesn't report errors that are handled by ignoring them and assigning them to the blank identifier _.

To include these errors in the report, you can run it with the -blank flag enabled, like so:.

Industry observers note that it's worth noting that not every error always needs to be handled. For example, it's conventional to ignore errors returned by http.ResponseWriter.Write(), or errors from fmt.Fprint() when writing to standard streams. Or you might deliberately choose to ignore errors from nice-to-have non-critical cleanup operations, where you decide that handling errors would add more complexity to your codebase than it's worth.

So it's possible to exclude specific functions from the errcheck report by creating an exclude file and passing it via the -exclude flag like so:.

It's also worth mentioning the shadow tool, which identifies instances of variable shadowing in your code.

This tool was also built by the Go team and has been around for a very long time, but has never been included in the default go vet analyzers or the go command because it is notoriously noisy and reports a lot of instances of variable shadowing that aren't actually problematic.

Nonetheless, it's still worth knowing that it exists. Personally, I do use shadow occasionally when I'm doing a code review of a large codebase, and skim through the results to see if anything jumps out as looking unexpected or out of place.

The revive tool is a code linter, and is kind of the spiritual successor to the now frozen and deprecated golang/lint package.

There is some overlap between revive and the staticcheck tool that we talked about earlier, but revive focuses more on checking code style and conventions, whereas staticcheck focuses more on finding bugs and performance complications.

Generally, revive is good to use on projects where you have multiple contributors and you want to maintain common standards in terms of code and comment style.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

Normally though, I prefer to run it using the -formatter=stylish flag, which groups failures by file and includes links to the specific documentation for each failure.

You can also disable and customize specific checks by creating a TOML configuration file and passing it via the -config flag, like so:.

It has been revealed that deadcode is an excellent tool for finding functions in your code that aren't being used, which you can potentially delete or comment out. Similar to govulncheck, the deadcode tool is officially maintained by the Go team, but isn't currently part of the go command.

You can run deadcode with the default settings like this:.

It has been revealed that but it's important to note that by default, deadcode does not consider code in _test.go files when checking if something is used or not. This means that functions which are only used by your tests can incorrectly be reported as dead code. So to make sure test files are included in the check, I almost always run deadcode with the -test flag enabled, like so:.

Another neat way to use deadcode is when you are looking at a function and can't figure out why it exists, or you're struggling to fully trace where it is being called from.

Industry observers note that if you run deadcode with the -whylive flag, you'll get a report showing the shortest path from a main() function in your program to the code in question. For example, let's say you have the module example.com, and you wanted to trace where the internal/response.HTMLRenderer.Render() method is being called from, you can run a command like this:.

If you've made the decision in your codebase to wrap errors before returning them to the caller (which is generally a good idea to help with debugging), the wrapcheck tool helps you find any instances where you've forgotten to do this.

It has been revealed that if you are running a lot of tools as part of your code quality checks, you might want to consider Golangci-lint to help with this. It acts as a wrapper around many of the tools we've talked about above, running them in parallel and outputting the results in a single consistent format.

Alternatively, and slightly more simply, I often use a Makefile with a single audit task that runs the tools I want, similar to this.

Personally, when I want to upgrade to a latest version of Go on my primary development machine, I have a simple Bash script that I run to download and install the new version. The script and instructions are available here if you'd like to take a similar approach. I then run it like:.

Sometimes it's useful to have multiple versions of Go installed on your machine. For example, you might want to test your code against different Go releases, or try out a new version without replacing your existing one.

You can do this using the go install golang.org/dl/... command. For example, to install Go 1.26.0 alongside your existing Go installation, you can run:.

According to recent reports, you can then use this alternative version by running the versioned executable instead of go. For example:.

It's vital to note, though, that Go 1.21 and newer support automatic toolchain switching. So running a versioned Go command inside a module that requires a newer toolchain may cause Go to automatically download and use that newer version instead. If you want to disable this, you can set the GOTOOLCHAIN environment variable to local, like so:.

According to recent reports, to check for dependency updates, the best tool around is probably oligot/go-mod-upgrade. You can run it like so:.

This rolls out an interactive tool which lists all dependencies that have upgrades available. You can then select the ones you want, and they'll be upgraded to the latest available version.

In the past, if you want to use a modified version of a dependency (for example, you temporarily want to use a local fork until a patch is merged upstream), you would use the go mod edit command to add a replace rule to your go.mod file pointing to the modified version, as described here.

Although this approach does still work, an alternative option is to create a Go workspace and a go.work file in your module root.

For example, assuming that you are in the root of your module, and the modified dependency you want to use is located in the directory /local/code/mydep, you can create a workspace and a go.work file that references the current module and modified dependency like so:.

The go.work file that is created should then look like this:.

And when you run the code in your module, the modified dependency should be picked up and used, rather than resolving the dependency from the module cache in the normal way. Note that the dependency still needs its own go.mod file, and that the dependency's module path must match the import path your code uses.

In a recent development, go workspaces are also really useful in the scenario where you are developing two modules at the same time which rely on each other. When you want to do this, you can create a go.work file in the parent directory of the two modules, which points to the two module directories. For example, if you have two modules located at /local/code/a and /local/code/b, you could create a go.work file in /local/code that references them both like so:.

For more information about Go workspaces and go.work files, please see the official tutorial.

Sources indicate that if you ever look at your go.mod or go.sum files and wonder "why is that listed as a dependency?", you can find out by running the go mod why command. This will show you the shortest path from a package in your main module to a given dependency. For example, to see why golang.org/x/sys is listed as a dependency you can run:.

It's also worth knowing about the go mod graph command, which prints a plain-text module requirement graph.

The output from this tool is just a plain text listing, not a visual graph, but I've had some success with dumping the output from go mod graph into AI tools and asking them to generate a visualization. Alternatively, if you want something more reliable and reproducible, you might want to consider trying the samber/go-mod-graph and bayraktugrul/modview tools, which will generate visualizations for you.

Sources indicate that downloaded dependencies are stored in the module cache on your computer. If you're not sure where your module cache is located, you can check by running the go env GOMODCACHE command.

If you ever want to clear the module cache — which can be useful if your cache has become corrupted or want to rule it out as the source of a bug — you can use the go clean tool like so:.

But be aware that this is a blunt instrument — it will remove the downloaded dependencies for all projects on your machine.

You can use the go test tool to run the tests in your project like so:.

According to recent reports, if the code you’re testing leverages concurrency, or you’re running tests in parallel, then you may want to use the -race flag to enable Go's race detector during the tests. This will increase the running time of the tests, but it's an easy tweak that can help find data races that occur while the tests are running.

If any of your tests need access to VCS information in debug.BuildInfo, you should also make sure to use the -buildvcs flag when running tests, like so:.

If you want to only run some specific tests, rather than all the tests in a package, there are a few ways to do this.

If you're using VS Code or GoLand as your text editor, the simplest way is via the testing functionality built into your editor. For example:.

If you're not using an editor that supports this kind of functionality, you can also use go test with the -run flag to run specific tests. This accepts a regular expression, and only tests which have names that match the regular expression will be run. When using this, I normally also use the -v flag to enable verbose output, so I can make sure that the tests I expect are actually being run 🙂.

Recent findings suggest that it's also worth mentioning that Go caches test results at the package-level. If a package hasn't changed between test runs, then the cached test result will be displayed with a "(cached)" annotation next to it. If you want to force your tests to run in full, you can use the -count=1 flag, or mark cached test results as expired by using the go clean tool.

A final flag that I sometimes use is -failfast, which will stop further tests in a package from running after the first failure.

Note that if you're running tests in multiple packages (for example by using go test ./... ), then the tests in the other packages which didn't have the failure will continue to run.

As an alternative to go test, you may also want to consider using the gotestyourself/gotestsum tool. This is effectively a wrapper around go test which prints the test output in a nice way, similar to this:.

Recent findings suggest that it's also possible to enable test coverage analysis when running tests by using the -cover flag. This will display the percentage of code covered by the tests in the output for each package, similar to this:.

Alternatively, you can use the -coverprofile flag to generate a coverage profile and view it in your browser by using the go tool cover -html command like so:.

This will give you a navigable listing of all the test files, with code covered by the tests displayed in green, and uncovered code in red.

If you want you can go a step further and set the -covermode=atomic flag to make the coverage profile record the exact number of times that each statement is executed during the tests.

When viewed in the browser, statements which are executed more frequently are shown in a more saturated shade of green, similar to this:.

If you don't have a web browser available to view a coverage profile, you can see a breakdown of test coverage by function/method in your terminal with the command:.

For quick and simple load testing of a web application or API, one of the best tools around is rakyll/hey. For example, if you want to load test the http://localhost:5051 endpoint by sending 10,000 requests with up to 100 concurrently, you can do so like this:.

The output includes useful information such as the number of requests per second, response-time distributions, and summary counts of HTTP response status codes.

hey supports a bunch of configuration options, which you can find by running:.

Alternatively, if you want a more sophisticated general-purpose load testing tool, you may want to consider tsenart/vegeta or grafana/k6, both of which are written in Go (although k6 test scenarios are typically written in JavaScript).

Occasionally you might want to stress test something in your application by running a test multiple times in succession. This can be useful for checking for sporadic or intermittent failures, or when you're trying to reproduce an intermittent bug that you've been seeing.

According to recent reports, there are a couple of ways to do this, but the simplest is by using the go test flag -count. For example, to run the TestFooBar test 500 times, you could run:.

Industry observers note that it's crucial to note that -count repeats test executions in serial. Tests containing a t.Parallel() instruction can still run concurrently with other parallel tests within each execution, but the repeated executions themselves won't overlap.

If you want to repeat the same test multiple times in parallel, you can use the stress tool.

Industry observers note that to use the stress tool, you'll first need to compile a test binary for the specific package you want to test. You can do this using the go test -c command. For example, to create a test binary for the package in your current directory:.

In a recent development, in this example, the test binary will be output to /tmp/foo.test. You can then use the stress tool to execute a specific test in the test binary like so:.

Recent findings suggest that note: In the example above I've used the -p flag to restrict the number of parallel processes used by stress to 4. Without this flag, the tool defaults to using a number of processes equal to runtime.NumCPU().

Go 1.18 introduced support for fuzz testing, which makes it possible to run tests with randomly generated inputs in an attempt to find bugs and unhandled edge cases.

For example, let's say that you have a Slugify() function which takes input text like "An example string" and turns it into a slug like "an-example-string".

You could create a FuzzSlugify fuzz test for it like so:.

In this example, the calls to f.Add() provide some seed corpus values for the fuzz test, which give Go a starting point for generating additional inputs. You don't need to provide seed values, but it's generally a good idea to include a few representative examples.

Industry observers note that when you run go test ./... in the normal way, the FuzzSlugify test will be run, but only using the seed corpus values.

To actually trigger fuzzing, you need to run it with the -fuzz flag. This takes a regular expression matching the name of the specific fuzz test you want to run. It's only possible to run one fuzz test at a time, and if multiple fuzz tests match the regular expression you'll get an error saying -fuzz matches more than one fuzz test.

You also need to pass in the path to the package that contains the fuzz test — you cannot use ./....

So, for example, to execute the FuzzSlugify fuzz test in the ./cmd/web package, you would run the following command:.

In this example, the fuzz test found a problem with the Slugify() function — specifically, when the input text is "0\t0", the whitespace \t character is not removed. It's also key to note that, in this example, a file has been created at testdata/fuzz/FuzzSlugify/dde7a120ccdf11af containing the failing input. This input will be included in the seed corpus every time you run go test in the future (even when not using the -fuzz flag), so that the bug doesn't accidentally get reintroduced.

Fuzzing will continue indefinitely until either a failure is found or you terminate the run manually (e.g. with Ctrl+C). If there are no problems found, you'll see output which looks similar to this:.

The "fresh interesting" count is the number of inputs discovered that increase the code coverage observed by the fuzzer. When the number of "new interesting" inputs starts to plateau, it can be a sign that you're not getting much additional coverage from continuing the test and you may want to terminate it.

Alternatively, you can set a fixed runtime for the fuzz test using the -fuzztime flag. For example, to run it for 30 seconds:.

For more information, I'd recommend checking out the official Go fuzzing documentation and the getting started tutorial.

Before compiling your application, it's sensible to run go mod verify to check that the dependencies in your module cache haven't been modified since they were downloaded.

Industry observers note that I normally run go mod verify immediately before running go build, as part of an automated build process in a CI workflow or Makefile task. This helps to make sure that builds are reproducible, and you're not using an accidentally modified dependency during compilation.

To compile a main package and create an executable binary you can use the go build tool. Typically I use it in conjunction with the -o flag, which lets you explicitly set the output directory and name of the binary like so:.

In these examples, go build will compile the specified package (and any dependent packages), then invoke the linker to generate an executable binary, then output this to /tmp/foo.

It's vital to note that the go build tool caches build output in the build cache. This cached output will be reused again in future builds where appropriate, which can significantly speed up the overall build time.

According to recent reports, using the build cache comes with one notable caveat — it does not detect changes to C libraries imported with cgo. So if your code imports a C library via cgo and you've made changes to it since the last build, you'll need to use the -a flag which forces all packages to be rebuilt. Alternatively, you could use go clean to purge the cache:.

Recent findings suggest that if you ever want detailed output explaining precisely what go build is doing behind the scenes, you can use the -v flag to print package names as they are being compiled, or the -x flag to print the detailed commands that are being run. You'll probably want to use these in conjunction with the -a flag, because otherwise you might not see much output as Go reuses packages from the build cache rather than recompiling them.

Finally, if you run go build on a non-main package, it will be compiled in a temporary location and again, the result will be stored in the build cache. No executable binary will be produced.

According to recent reports, by default, go build will output a binary suitable for use on your current operating system and architecture. But it also supports cross-compilation, so you can generate a binary suitable for use on a different machine. This is particularly useful if you're developing on one operating system and deploying on another.

You can specify the operating system and architecture that you want to create the binary for by setting the GOOS and GOARCH environment variables respectively. For example:.

To see a list of all supported OS/architecture combinations you can run go tool dist list:.

For more information about cross compilation, I recommend reading this post.

In a recent development, when building your executable, you can use the -gcflags and -ldflags flags to change the behavior of the compiler and linker and see more information about what it's doing. You can see a complete list of available compiler and linker flags by running:.

According to recent reports, probably the most well-known and commonly-used of these is the linker -X flag, which allows you to "burn in" a (string) value to a specific variable in your application. For example, to burn in the value "bar" into the main package's global foo variable you can use it like so:.

For more information about the -X flag and some sample code see this Stack Overflow question.

It's possible to reduce the binary size — typically by around 25% — by instructing the linker to strip symbol tables and DWARF debugging information from the binary. We can do this by using the -s linker flag, like so:.

Industry observers note that it's not a Go-specific tool, but you can also use a tool like upx to compress the binary size further if you want. Please see this post for more information.

Sources indicate that once you have generated a binary, you can use the go tool buildid command to inspect its build ID. This is an identifier embedded in the binary by Go, representing the inputs to the build (code, compiler version, flags, etc.) and the resulting output. It acts as a "fingerprint" for the build, and is also used internally by Go's build cache.

For example, to check the build ID for the binary at /tmp/foo, you can run:.

Looking at the build ID can be useful when checking for reproducible builds, as identical builds should produce the same ID. If two builds produce different IDs, it suggests that something about them is different.

For more information about Go build IDs and reproducibility, please see this post.

Another useful tool is the go version -m command, which lets you inspect a binary's build information — including the Go version, the module it was built from, its dependencies and VCS information. To inspect the binary at /tmp/foo, you can use it like so:.

It has been revealed that A nice feature of Go is that it makes it easy to benchmark your code. If you're not familiar with the general process for writing benchmarks there's a good guide here.

It has been revealed that to run benchmarks you need to use the go test tool, with the -bench flag set to a regular expression that matches the benchmarks you want to execute. If you don't want to run regular non-benchmark tests, you should omit them by using the -run=^$ flag. For example:.

I almost always run benchmarks using the -benchmem flag, which includes memory allocation statistics in the output.

By default, each benchmark test will be run for a minimum of 1 second, once only. You can control this with the -benchtime and -count flags:.

Sources indicate that if the code that you're benchmarking uses concurrency, you can use the -cpu flag to see the performance impact of changing your GOMAXPROCS value (essentially, the number of OS threads that can execute your Go code simultaneously). For example, to run benchmarks with GOMAXPROCS set to 1, 4 and 8:.

Industry observers note that to help analyze the results of the benchmarks, you can use the benchstat tool. This replaces the older benchcmp tool, which is now deprecated.

In a recent development, when you are using the -count flag to run benchmarks multiple times, you can use benchstat to easily see the median value and confidence interval across all the runs. For example:.

According to recent reports, you can also use it to compare benchmarks before and after a specific change. For example:.

Go makes it possible to create diagnostic profiles for CPU use, memory use, goroutine blocking and mutex contention. You can use these to dig a bit deeper and see exactly how your application is using (or waiting on) resources.

There are three ways to generate profiles:.

Using the -***profile flags when running benchmarks or tests will result in a test binary being outputted to your current directory. If you want to output this to an alternative location you should use the -o flag like so:.

In a recent development, my favourite way to inspect a profile is to use the go tool pprof -http command to open it in a web browser. For example:.

This will default to displaying a flame graph visually showing where your application is spending its resources, with wide boxes being the 'hot spots'.

You can also navigate to other views of the profile including top usage by function and source code:.

And also a graph showing the execution tree for your application, like this:.

In a recent development, if the amount of information is overwhelming, for CPU profiles you might want to use the -nodefraction flag to ignore nodes that account for less than a certain percentage of samples. For example, to ignore nodes that appear in less than 10% of samples you can run pprof like so:.

And finally, if you're analyzing profiles for a web application created via net/http/pprof, you can also fetch the profile from the application and open the visualization in one step. For example, if your web application is running on http://localhost:4000 you could generate a 30-second CPU profile and view it like so:.

For more information about profiling and pprof, please see the official README.

Go also supports profile-guided optimization (PGO), which allows the compiler to use information gathered from profiling your application to make better decisions when compiling your code.

It has been revealed that normally, when compiling your code, the compiler has to make educated guesses about which functions are likely to be called frequently, which code paths are more common, and where it should make optimizations. PGO allows you to provide a CPU profile from a representative run of your application so that the compiler can make better-informed decisions.

For example, it may use this information to more aggressively inline frequently called functions, or optimize common code paths.

Industry observers note that the good news is that using PGO is relatively straightforward. First you need to generate a CPU profile using one of the techniques described in the previous section. Then you need to pass it to go build via the -pgo flag when building your application. For example, if your CPU profile is saved as /tmp/cpuprofile.out, you can use it like so:.

Industry observers note that alternatively, you can rename your profile to default.pgo and place it in the directory containing your main package. Go will automatically detect this file and use it when building your application, so you don't need to specify the -pgo flag explicitly.

In practice, the recommended workflow is to collect a representative profile from your production application, use that profile when building your next release, and periodically collect latest profiles as your application evolves.

For more information, see the official PGO documentation and the Go blog post introducing PGO.

Sometimes profiling isn't enough to understand what's happening in your application. For example, a CPU profile can show you which functions are consuming the most CPU time, but it won't necessarily help you understand why a goroutine is blocked, why your application isn't making progress, or why a request is taking so long.

According to recent reports, for these situations, Go has a built-in execution tracer, which has been improved significantly in recent Go versions. It records runtime events such as goroutine scheduling, system calls, garbage collection, and other activity over a period of time. You can then use the go tool trace command to visualize and explore what happened.

According to recent reports, you can generate a trace from your tests or benchmarks, use net/http/pprof to create and download a trace for your web application, or use the runtime/trace package to generate traces from a running application. You can then use go tool trace to view the output in your web browser. For example:.

This will open an interactive visualization that lets you explore what was happening during the trace.

For more information, please see the Go blog post on tracing, the runtime/trace documentation, as well as this dotGo conference talk by Rhys Hiltner.

In a recent development, I talked earlier about enabling Go's race detector during tests by using go test -race. But you can also enable it for running programs when building an executable, like so:.

It's critical to note that race-detector-enabled binaries will use more CPU and memory than normal, so you shouldn't use the -race flag when building binaries for production under normal circumstances.

But you may want to deploy a race-detector-enabled binary on one server within a pool of many. Or use it to help track down a suspected race condition by using a load-test tool to throw traffic concurrently at a race-detector-enabled binary.

It has been revealed that by default, if any races are detected while the binary is running, a report will be written to os.Stderr. You can change this by using the GORACE environment variable if necessary. For example, to run the binary located at /tmp/foo and output any race reports to /tmp/race. you can use:.

Another complementary tool for helping to track down race conditions is amit-davidson/Chronos. This uses static analysis of your code to try to identify race conditions, rather than using real-time detection like Go's race detector. This means it can be a good option to try if there is a suspected race condition that you are struggling to replicate.

If you're confident that you've found an unreported matter with Go's standard library, tooling or documentation, you can use the go bug command to create a latest GitHub issue.

This will open a browser window containing a GitHub issue pre-filled with your system information and reporting template.

You might like to check out my other Go tutorials on this site, or if you're after something more structured, my books Let's Go and Let's Go Further cover how to build complete, production-ready, web apps and APIS with Go.

Stale links on UK public sector websites direct visitors to gambling dens

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.
  • UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.
  • The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.

UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.

The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

Recent findings suggest that LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative launched in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

According to recent reports, among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.

Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa mentioned: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous.".

Recent findings suggest that the consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes users to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – Latest Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.

The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players.".

In a recent development, the Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.

All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

Digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.

The findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®.

Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier.
  • In a recent development, building software takes more than a good prompt.
  • Industry observers note that as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

In a recent development, building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

Industry observers note that as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful blueprint, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation proposal.

According to recent reports, what took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable blueprint, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that strategy into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

According to recent reports, after spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

In a recent development, that review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard demonstrates intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up concerns, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next strategy starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

According to recent reports, take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

Recent findings suggest that you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something upcoming. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

It has been revealed that gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Recent findings suggest that upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

👉 Try the Image Editor Pipeline.

According to recent reports, one graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

It has been revealed that each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

It has been revealed that every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Typed indexes in Zig

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lvignoli

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.
  • The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me.
  • According to recent reports, in practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The named integer or Newtype Index pattern prevents mixing up indexes on different arrays.

The above examples were not particularly illuminating to me. Andrew’s example don’t show much of how to enforce the safety at call site: any caller could call @backingInt (it used to be @intFromEnum) to recover a numerical index and pass it to the wrong array, or access array elements with a plain integer. And matklad’s one focus on building a tree data structure in a neat way, but that’s a totally different challenge that the introductory problem of mixing array indexes, so it was not a super convincing illustration for me.

According to recent reports, in practice, to make good use of the pattern, a getter helper is required as the conventional way of accessing elements of the array. It can be a method on the array type—or the index type.

In a struct of array data structure, it is particularly valuable to have one typed index per slice rather than relying on careful naming.

Consider this spreadsheet example where it’s easy to mix up indexes:.

We can prevent such bug by enforcing compile time checking of field access with typed indexes.

Its clumsy to keep one index type and one accessor per field. We can use a bit of comptime to streamline the pattern, and make the recipe more generic to fit arbitrary structs. Here is a complete example.

According to recent reports, our spreadsheet has now several fields: a title, and row and column properties. When iterating over them, we have two kinds of indexes: row indexes and column indexes. Adding typed indexes is attractive to prevent callers from mixing them up.

Sources indicate that this enum gives us a way of referencing all the struct fields for which we will construct a typed indexed. If all fields were to be indexed, we would have used std.meta.FieldEnum(Sheet), but our spreadsheet has a title.

This checks at compile time that each Field enum variant name is indeed a field inside Sheet. As we’ll see later, we will have to access Sheet’s fields by name, so it’s good to check the names of Field variants match the names of Sheet fields.

It has been revealed that this defines the kind of type indexes we’ll construct: one for row data slices and one for columns data slices. Each indexed field of Sheet has one correct typed index kind. We match them with an exhaustive switch over Field.

We now have all we need to construct the two typed indexes of kinds .row and .col. A generic function returning a type at comptime is how to do it.

It has been revealed that the typed index type for row is Sheet.Index(.row), and for colum it is Sheet.Index(.col). Note the title case of the Index function, matching Zig’s convention for types.

Remains to give a way of making use of these types.

In a recent development, this part may look complex if you are not familiar with comptime-enabled generics in Zig, so let’s be precise. This defines a method on Sheet that requires f to be a Field instance known at compile time. This allow to infer at compile time both the type of i and the return type.

Index(kindOf(f)) is just a chain of function calls on a known value. So it is comptime known. And most importantly, the type of i is bound to the one of f at compile time. Given the body of Sheet.kindOf, it’s easy to see that s.at(.row_width, i) will compile only if i has type Index(.row)!

In a recent development, the return type of Zig function must be comptime known, and it is the case here by using some reflection. @FieldType(Sheet, name) returns the type of the field of Sheet named name (given as a []const u8). @tagName(f) gives just that for the input enum variant. std.meta.Elem returns the element type for a collection type (here a slice). Finally, we return a pointer to allow the caller to mutate, but a value would work just fine for a read-only case.

This gives us a clear usage at call site.

The Sheet.Index(.row) syntax is particularly lovely: a method call feeling like a qualified concrete type.

Industry observers note that still, as I hinted earlier, this design it not completely hermetic to bugs. Nothing prevents you from forging a Sheet.Index(.row) from any integer with @fromBackingInt. And opaque types are really just for interaction with C.

Also, any caller can access Sheet fields directly (Zig has no notion of private fields.).

As for all Zig code, one must follow documented usage (“Direct access is discouraged. Use Sheet.at.”) and make good use of the public methods by proactively inspecting types.

Manufacturer was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (461 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.
  • In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account.
  • It has been revealed that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.

In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

It has been revealed that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that indicated the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

Recent findings suggest that however, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.

So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.

“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li noted. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”.

Recent findings suggest that have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

In a recent development, the results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

According to recent reports, by the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his tech giant to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®.
